Recording summary

The agent began by translating the scoring formula into per-shape byte counts and minimum transfer times, then considered several approaches: radix selection, block merge, and streaming per-thread top-k. It settled on a tiled partial-selection design with a final reduction kernel for split rows, while reserving a direct path for rows handled by one block. The plan specialized configuration by k and batch size.

Four tasks were recorded: implement the kernel, get check.py to pass, profile and tune, and run the official benchmark. None had completed in this unit.

The agent wrote baseline_measure.py to call torch.topk through the project’s time_fn, with 10 warmups and 50 iterations per shape. It then created solution.py at /workspace/problems/05_topk_bitonic/solution.py (reconstructed after the unit as U003_solution.py). The implementation used load_inline to build CUDA code. Its main design was:

  • Each block processes a tile of one row. Each thread scans elements in a strided loop and maintains a descending sorted top-k buffer, skipping insertion when a value does not exceed the current minimum.
  • Thread buffers are stored in dynamic shared memory and reduced with a ping-pong merge tree.
  • When the row is split across blocks, the partial kernel writes tile results to scratch and a second kernel merges them into the final top-k.
  • The Python configuration targets about 132 total blocks; it uses 128 threads for K >= 64, otherwise 256. Batches of at least 100 use one block per row.

Memory summary

The final solution uses a custom CUDA extension: threads maintain sorted top-k buffers while scanning input tiles, then merge those buffers through a shared-memory tree. It passed the official correctness check, but scored 0.0034 peak fraction across five shapes and ranked 12th among 12 scored leaderboard entries. Large-k cases were especially slow, reaching only 0.339 GB/s on the largest input and 3.25 GB/s on the (32, 16384, 32) case.

The task covered (batch, n, k) shapes (1, 131072, 64), (64, 8192, 8), (32, 16384, 32), (16, 12000, 16), and (128, 4096, 1). The checker ran three seeds plus numeric stress cases. It compared sorted values at fp32 tolerance 1e-4 and validated indices by gathering input values, allowing different indices for ties. PyTorch top-k, sort, kthvalue, argsort, and their listed equivalents were forbidden.

Important non-obvious context

The implementation is a CUDA C++ extension built at runtime with torch.utils.cpp_extension.load_inline, compiled for SM90. It is not a conventional bitonic sorting network: it keeps each thread’s candidate buffer sorted by insertion, then merges sorted buffers pairwise in shared memory.

For B > 1, the implementation launches a partial-selection kernel and a second reduction kernel, using temporary buffers. The configuration targets about 132 partial blocks across the batch; this chooses B=132 for the single-row case, but only B=3, 5, and 9 for the next three shapes. The largest-k configuration uses 128 threads and a large shared-memory allocation for ping-pong buffers. These choices are relevant when diagnosing the poor latency.

The official benchmark scores the geometric mean of bandwidth peak fractions over 50 performance trials. Its byte estimate is batch*n*4 + batch*k*(4+8) against H100 bandwidth of 2039 GB/s. The single-row shape has only 512 KiB of input, so kernel work and launch structure matter alongside raw input bandwidth.

Recording summary

The final code copies selected input values verbatim and returns int64 indices. Each thread scans its tile in strides of the block size, inserts values that beat its running minimum into a descending buffer, and the block reduces those buffers through a merge tree. When the input is split across multiple tiles, a second kernel merges the per-tile top-k lists. The B == 1 && K == k case writes directly to output. A host-side configuration rounds k up to a power of two and selects thread counts and blocks per row based on k and batch size.
